Further analysis of the in-cylinder pressure traces revealed that plasma activation caused a transient increase in the coefficient of variation in cylinder peak pressure during the initial cycles. This effect was attributed to the engine’s individual cylinder control (ICC) system adjusting fuel distribution to accommodate the modified combustion characteristics of the reformed fuel. As the ICC system adapted, pressure uniformity stabilized, demonstrating that the plasma reformer did not induce sustained instability. Overall, the AJAX 2802 engine tests confirmed that the plasma reformer effectively reduced methane leaks and enhanced combustion efficiency without requiring hardware modifications to the engine. The low reformer power consumption (400 W average) validated that the technology operates below the 1 percent engine energy target. Future testing on the AJAX engine was planned to evaluate reformer integration on the main fuel line rather than the pre-chamber fuel line. However, due to limited engine availability at Cooper Machinery Services during the test period, these additional experiments could not be completed. Consequently, an alternate engine at SwRI (Cummins X15N) was used to assess methane leak reduction in a configuration without a prechamber. 3.5 Engine Testing on the Cummins X15N To evaluate plasma reformer performance without pre-chambers and at higher engine speeds and transient operating conditions, additional testing was performed on a Cummins X15N six- cylinder natural-gas engine. This engine, rated at 400 bhp and operating at approximately 1,900 rpm, represents a typical heavy-duty configuration. This test campaign evaluated the reformer’s effect on methane leaks, combustion characteristics, and power efficiency in a smaller- displacement, high-speed engine typical of heavy-duty transportation and industrial applications. The reformer was installed in-line with the X15N’s natural-gas supply system, positioned upstream of the intake manifold to ensure uniform distribution of reformed fuel to all cylinders. Due to the increased EMI potential at higher pulse repetition frequencies, the reformer assembly was wrapped in conductive shielding and grounded to prevent signal coupling with nearby engine sensors and communication circuits. Figure 19 shows the integrated test setup, including the Cummins X15N engine and the plasma reformer enclosed within the metallic shielding used to mitigate EMI effects during operation. Cummins X15N engine (left) and plasma reformer installation (right) used for high-speed testing. The reformer was enclosed in conductive shielding to minimize EMI during pulsed-plasma operation at frequencies up to 100 kHz. Testing was conducted under full-load steady-state conditions at a fixed air–fuel ratio (λ = 1). The plasma duty cycle was varied between 50%, 75%, and 100%, while methane leaks were monitored continuously using a Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) analyzer. Baseline testing without plasma operation recorded a steady methane concentration of approximately 959 parts per million (ppm). When the plasma was active, methane slip decreased to 700–900 ppm, corresponding to reductions between 6 and 27 percent, depending on power level and duty cycle.
